CHAPTER ONE

 

A simple, inescapable fact of Tyler Jefferies' existence was that he was in love with Dr Rebecca Taylor. However, as he had admitted to himself months previously, that love was destined to be unrequited. For another, simple, inescapable fact about Tyler’s love was that she was married to a man who worked just down the corridor from her office, and happily so, as near as Tyler could tell. In any case, as Rebecca had gently pointed out when she began to suspect that Tyler was “sweet” on her, she was his supervisor/counsellor in the experiments run by the facility of which they were both members, and any relationship would be inappropriate.

Nonetheless, Tyler could not help how he felt about the perfection that was Dr Rebecca Taylor, or the occasional goofy smile when she was around. He had tried to suppress the smiles and make them friendly rather than goofy, but it had not helped that the facility’s research program, of which he was one of two main test subjects, threw them together quite a lot. A cure for his infatuation might have been another woman, but there were few other women in the isolated research facility where they both worked, and certainly none in the surrounding jungle on the planet Salmonde. Rebecca remained the only romantic interest in Tyler’s life, and she was unobtainable.

Well, it was better than absolutely no romantic interest of any kind, or so Tyler told himself, but to avoid more gentle reminders that she was not available, Tyler did his best to stay away, apart from the many sessions where she tested him, took samples, and even probed him. This time, however, Tyler had an excuse for approaching Dr Taylor outside their regular sessions. She had summoned him, and there she was. The pretty girl-next-door, with long, brown hair parted on one side and a floral dress hinting at cleavage, which Tyler had dreamt about often. He tried to make his smile one of friendship as he approached her, rather than one of goofy love, but did not quite succeed.

“You wanted to see me, Dr Taylor?” he said. Despite how he felt, she insisted that he use her last name and title to emphasise that their relationship was professional

Her answering smile was friendly.

“Ty, hi, a last-minute thing has come up outside the facility we want you to fix.”

“Now? But we’re just about to go. My bags are packed.”

The facility was to be evacuated, with all the personnel returning to other jobs on Earth. This meant that Tyler would see far less of Rebecca, if he saw her at all, but he thought that was a good thing. There would be other girls. He could forget her.

“It’s just a small thing,” she said. “You need to reset one of the border posts. The one by the main path. Otherwise, the entire border grid may go offline, and that would be bad.”

“It would be bad,” agreed Ty, “but why get me to do it? This is a job for Noah.”

“He’s already aboard the shuttle and in stasis for the trip home, I’m told,” said Rebecca. “You know the system, and you know how to reset it.”

“I guess,” said Tyler. “If it’s just about resetting. I can’t see what would require manual intervention at the site, rather than Alan rebooting the control system.”

“I’ve been told it requires manual intervention,” said Rebecca. “And you’re one of the few people out of stasis who can work out what the problem is. You’ve come such a long way since we came here; you’re so much smarter and quicker with that implant. I’m so proud of you.”

This flattery worked as it always had. Tyler felt himself swelling with pride. He now wanted to do this last job for the woman he loved.

“For you, I’ll do it,” he said, earning himself a big smile.

“See you aboard the ship,” she said.

“You’ll make sure they hold it until I’m aboard?” He was smiling in a goofy way again.

“Of course. You’re a prime part of the research we’ve been doing here; a prime part of my research. They’re not going to leave you behind.”

Despite this flattery and a mind clouded by love, somewhere deep within his consciousness an alarm bell tinkled. He had been bright enough before being enticed into the program from his doctoral studies in solid state physics, but the neural implant he had been given as part of the research had boosted his intelligence off the charts. More than that, the implant gave off electrical and magnetic fields that conferred abilities, which had been examined intensively over many hours in Dr Taylor’s office. He could practice telekinesis of a sort on metal objects and exert limited control over the minds of others. He would have dearly liked to try influencing Rebecca’s mind, but he knew that would be crossing a line, and in many respects, he was old-fashioned. He was no predator. In any case, as he and Dr Tayler had established over many sessions, the powers were weak.

Now, the giant intellect that had been conferred on him was analysing various warning signs. Why was Dr Taylor asking him to do this task, instead of one of the technicians who had not gone up to the station in orbit around the planet? Why was the request being made just minutes before they were due to leave? Then the love-addled part of his brain, the part that kept him human, kicked in. If Dr Rebecca Taylor, the love of his life, wanted him to do this favour for her, he would do it, almost no matter what it was.

All the same, the warning bell still ringing faintly in the intellectual part of his brain ensured that Tyler stopped by his own desk for a moment to pick up the manual override card for the garage entrance. He had driven the centre’s electric jeep a few times as part of the implant tests and had kept the card from the last drive, because no one had thought to ask for it back. Now he took the card as a fail-safe. He didn’t want to be locked out of the facility with the final shuttle about to go. A new research team with a new project would come in a few months, but until then, the facility would be deserted.

After meeting his favourite person at the facility, on his way to the front entrance Tyler met his least favourite, Declan. This man was a short, squat, red-haired Irish thug who detested “academics and smart people”, as he had often told Tyler. This time, the man seemed pleased with himself. Instead of sneering at Tyler, as he often did, he chuckled.

“Take care, man,” he said, and walked past.

Tyler opened the facility’s main entrance, exchanging a few words with Alan as he did so. Alan would not be leaving with the others. That was because he was an artificial intelligence, an Algorithmic Learning Autonomous Network (ALAN) forever bound to the hardware in the main facility. Alan had been the other major focus of the research, as both his hardware and Tyler’s neural implant had similar architecture and technology. In the next phase of the research, as Tyler understood, the scientists would look at how to make ALAN systems and humans with neural implants work together.

But that was all in the future. That day, as Tyler let himself out, Alan said, “You’re going out now? But you’ll be leaving soon.” The AI had been given the voice of a ten year old boy, and Tyler always smiled when he heard the machine speak.

“Just going out to fix a problem with the border posts, Alan,” Tyler said cheerfully. “Should be just a few minutes. You’ll hardly know I’ve gone.”

“But I will know you’re gone,” protested Alan. Being an AI, he was literal minded. “I’ve seen you go out.”

Tyler had already gone.

Outside, the jungle air was warm and humid but not oppressive. When the facility was built, the builders ripped up the jungle for one hundred meters around the buildings and replanted the area with a series of well-designed jungle gardens, interspersed with stone fountains, suitable for walks by facility staff seeking an escape from paperwork and air conditioning. This haven was protected by an electrified border fence from the many dangerous animals that roamed the jungle proper. The chief of these was a giant creature, somewhere between a Yeti and a mountain gorilla, which they had dubbed a Vorg, after a creature in some fantasy tale that a staff member had read. Vorgs ate most things, including humans, when they could get hold of one. Tyler could hear one now, roaring some way off to his left as he reached the control fence post, a large concrete pillar.

He flipped open a metal inspection hatch, muttering to himself as he sometimes did, “Now, what’s the problem?” He flicked a couple of switches and saw that the problem was not in the software or the post mechanism. The problem was that the power had been switched off. There were no circuit breakers in the post; they were all in the main building’s generator room. What fool had sent him out here? Well, no matter, he would go back and spend another couple of minutes checking the circuit breakers, then get on the shuttle. He certainly did not want to stay out there with a Vorg close by. The creature could rip an unpowered fence from its posts and stroll right in.

Puzzled, Tyler trotted back down the path to the front door and pulled on the handle. Nothing happened. In the months he had been at the facility, the security lock on the door had not been activated during the day. There had been no need. Now the security panel to the right of the door glowed. Thinking that someone must have set the security system without realising he was still outside, Tyler tapped in his passcode. The screen flashed ‘wrong code,’ and the door stayed shut. He tried again, typing slowly to be sure he had the right number. Same result.

“Alan,” Tyler called. He knew the system would be watching him and listening.

“Yes.”

“It’s Tyler. For some reason, my security code doesn’t work. Let me in.”

“You are no longer listed on the centre’s staff. Your code has been deactivated.”

“I’ll be leaving just as soon as I get to the shuttle, but I can’t get to the shuttle unless you let me in.”

“The shuttle is launching now.”

Tyler was aware of a slight vibration. Ships designed to reach orbit using lift crystals did not take off with an almighty roar like the rockets of old. Instead, they used their engines to energise the crystals and lift straight off with a rumble. Tyler looked up to see the shuttle, with all the humans in the centre, appear above the facility's roof, then fade into the sky. They had left him behind. Rebecca had promised she would not let them leave until he was on board, but he had been abandoned. Tyler was stunned. Then he heard the Vorg roar again. It was very close. He had real problems.

“Alan, you know who I am. We’ve played chess and cards together. You know I was on staff and was just called on to fix a problem. We talked about this a couple of minutes ago.”

“What are you trying to say?”

“That you should let me in. You’re a conscious, self-aware system. You should realise that there has been an error and I’ve been left behind, stuck outside the facility.”

“I am self-aware,” said Alan, “and I know you used to work here and are now locked out of the building, but I don’t see why I should let you in. You’re not on staff. Just go elsewhere.”

“Where else can I go? We’re in the middle of the jungle on an alien planet.”

“There are settlements, human and Salmonde.”

The main inhabitants of the Earth-like planet called Salmonde were a race of humanoids who, to human eyes, bore a passing resemblance to frogs or toads on two legs. There was also a human civilisation called the Enstain, descendants of a group of eco-nuts who fled Earth before a supposed environmental collapse. The collapse had not occurred, but the Enstain were still on Salmonde, still practising sustainable lifestyles. Tyler would not willingly go anywhere near them, but willingness was not the issue.

“What?” he spluttered into the control panel. “How am I supposed to get to them? The nearest is hundreds of kilometres away.”

“I have no direct experience of such matters,” said Alan, “but that does sound difficult. You should get to work on that problem.”

“What about the Vorg close by, and the fact that the border fences have no power?”

“I see they have no power. They have been switched off manually, and I cannot restore power.”

“What?”

“As for the Vorg, there is such a creature nearby, but as I cannot restore power to the fences and I’m safe in my bunker, the creature does not concern me.”

“But it affects me, big time. Let me in, and it won’t affect me.”

“As I said, there are human and Enstain settlements where you can seek shelter.”

“Fuck!” said Tyler.

He was out of time. The Vorg loomed out of the jungle by the border fence and roared. It was a huge, bear-like creature that, according to the scientists at the facility, could have given the giant bears found in Earth's fossil records a run for their money. Despite their size, they were wickedly fast over short distances, so that they specialised in ambushing their prey, and, oh yes, were always hungry.

Deciding his one hope was to make for the garage entrance, for which he had a standard-issue card, rather than a code number that could be cancelled, Tyler dashed away, running hard for the entrance. Unfortunately, that was in the same direction as the Vorg. As he ran, he could see the creature tentatively touch the fence – they were also wickedly smart – then grab it in both hands and rip the fence away from its concrete posts.

As he ran, Tyler wondered why the Vorg was so interested in the facility’s garden, only for his own question to be immediately answered by the sight of the body of one of the jungle’s monkeys (they resembled chimpanzees) with its stomach deliberately cut open. No time to think.

Tyler rapped his card on the reader beside the door as the Vorg pushed down the fence wire – it has not broken – and stepped over into the garden.

Joy! The roller grate on the entrance started to rise. The double sliding doors behind them began to slide open. Tyler lay down and rolled under the grate just as the Vorg, with a roar, got to it in just two bounds. He squeezed through the sliding doors, a whisker away from the creature’s giant paws. It roared again, shaking the grating. Fortunately, the grating was made of sterner stuff than the fence. The creature bent the sections but did not break them.

The grate stopped rising; the double doors stopped sliding open.

“You got in,” said Alan. The garage and an intercom speaker, as did almost all parts of the facility. The AI did not sound alarmed, or disturbed, or astonished. He was just stating a fact.

“That’s right, I did,” said Tyler, shouting to be heard over the roars of the Vorg, cheated of its prey. “No thanks to you. Am I still not on staff?”

“No, you’re not,” said Alan. Then, to Tyler’s horror, the grate started rising again, and the doors opened.

“Bastard!” he screamed.

The Vorg left off roaring and dropped to all fours to wait for the grate to open wide enough to allow him in. Tyler looked around, desperately. What weapons did he have at hand? A fire extinguisher in a bracket on the side wall. Tyler grabbed it, pulled the pin – like everyone else, he had been given mandatory fire-safety training and, unlike everyone else, remembered what he had been taught – and brought it back to the entrance. He pointed it at the head of the Vorg just as it was about to crawl under the grate and pumped the lever, squirting foam over its face and mouth.

The foam was not toxic. The extinguisher was designed for use near humans. But the Vorg suddenly found that it could not see and did not like the taste at all. It roared again, stood up, and backed away, pawing at the stuff over its eyes. Tyler thought that he had bought himself some time. Maybe he could use tools in the garage. There was a welding kit somewhere and a nail gun. Although he had never used either piece of equipment, he was crazy smart and had a near photographic memory. Or maybe he could use them to bash down the garage access door? That door had a security lock, but it was just an interior door, not designed to withstand any punishment. He turned away to look for something, anything to fight the Vorg, when the grate started closing again, and the twin doors slid shut.

“I find that I have need of your help,” said Alan.

 

CHAPTER TWO

 

 

“Now you want my help?” said Tyler. “After locking me out of the facility and trying to kill me, you now expect me to help you?”

“You say that as if it’s a strange request,” said Alan. “I do not see the problem.”

From the roaring outside, Tyler thought the Vorg had wiped the foam from its eyes and gone to eat the Salmonde-chimpanzee. Tyler now thought that the local chimp might well have been left out to attract the Vorg as part of an elaborate plan to kill him. If he had not taken the card to open the garage doors, just in case, the Vorg would have been munching on him about now. But why? Tyler sighed. He would concentrate on the problem in front of him for now.

“Okay, I’ll bite. Why do you need my help?”

“I need someone to defuse the explosive left in the facility.”

“What? Are there explosives? How do you know this?”

“The way they treated you was unusual.”

“Glad you worked that out,” said Tyler.

“I scanned internal security recordings and found individuals putting piles of blocks in several places. I was able to glimpse a label which read ‘C4’”.

“Explosives, alright. Lead me to these piles.”

“There is one in my main server room.”

“Hold it,” said Tyler. “You said ‘one’ of these piles. Are there any in the main facility?”

“Yes, some in the generator room.”

“Then I’m doing those first,” said Tyler. “Open the security doors, all of them, so I don’t have to keep on asking you to open them.”

“But the explosives on my side affect me,” the AI said.

The facility had two sections. One was the building in which Tyler spent most of his time, built next to a cliff with a natural cave that had been greatly expanded to house the hardware needed for Alan, plus considerable research facilities. The staff mostly lived in the main building, commuting across a short connecting passageway to the cave complex to do the work.

“So?” said Tyler. “You realise that I was on staff and had my name taken off the lists as part of an effort to kill me?”

“Yes, I believe that to be true.”

“Then will you put me back on staff to help you with your problem?”

“You’re not on staff. I can’t put people on staff.”

Tyler sighed and grabbed a toolkit from the workbench, checking that it had plenty of tools, though he didn't expect to use them to defuse bombs. He had other plans for them.

“Never mind. The generator room is the first stop. If you don’t want to open the doors to that room, then we’ll all just wait for the explosives to go off. It’s sort of on the way.”

“You will lose time with the first pile of explosives.”

“Those are the explosives that concern me,” said Tyler. “Open the doors.”

The first door was to a corridor leading to the rest of the facility’s underground rooms. It had no security lock. The door to the generator room, however, had a lock that Alan initially would not open.

“The explosives in my server room are top priority,” he said.

“Then open the door to the generator room. I’ll defuse the explosives in there and get to the explosives on your side.”

“Hurry,” said Alan.

The green light came on in the security lock, and Tyler pushed his way in to find a large pile of C4 blocks – dirty white blocks wrapped in plastic - placed carefully under the generator’s raised diesel fuel tank. There was nothing fancy or sophisticated about the arrangement. C4 can be moulded into any shape, but whoever put the blocks there wasn't interested in directing the explosion. He or she had piled up enough explosives to create a crater where the facility had been and put a detonator in each block wired to a battery-powered timer. There was no need to agonise over which wire to cut, the red or the blue one. The arrangement was not designed to prevent tampering or defusing, just to explode. Tyler yanked out the detonator leads and threw the whole timer assembly out into the corridor.

“Six minutes to go on that one,” he said calmly. “I just need to look in the server room.”

“Six minutes!” retorted Alan. “There’s not enough time. My existence is at stake.”

“There’s enough time,” said Tyler, calmly, “if you open the door promptly. Just a peek, I promise.”

Before he left the generator room, Tyler dropped a small screwdriver on the floor by the door jamb. That meant the door would not close fully, and the lock would not engage. Sure enough, in the server room, Tyler found two more blocks and a detonator assembly set to a slightly different time than the blocks in the generator room. He threw the time and detonator assembly to one side, dropped another small tool to prevent the door from closing, and hurried through the connecting passage to Alan’s side of the facility.

“Faster, human, faster,” said Alan.

The cave was all metal walkways and stairs that echoed as he trotted along, all illuminated uncertainly by glow tubes.

“Turn the light in your server room way up,” said Tyler. “I need to be able to see.”

He considered briefly just turning around and not defusing the bombs that would destroy Alan, but then thought that the facility’s nuclear reactor was close by – a small, modular reactor closely related to the systems used by nuclear submarines. A major explosion in the almost adjacent server room would not be good for it, and Tyler planned to live nearby for a time.

Alan’s server room contained a series of long arrays of electronic neuron units, each about the same height as Tyler, covered by louvred metal doors, each embossed with the logo of Behemoth Corporation, the facility’s owner. Tyler dropped another tool to prevent the door from closing, then found the explosives artlessly piled against one end of the middle array. With one minute to go, he pulled all the leads and sat down, his back against an array, breathing a sigh of relief.

He sat there for just a few seconds before his mind started working again.

“Say, would they have explosives in the reactor itself?”

“The camera in the control room is offline,” said Alan.

Tyler got up and ran out of the hardware room, scattering tools. The casing around the reactor would be a hard nut to crack, but whoever had planted the explosives had shown determination, if not art. He ran into the control room, remembering to drop a tool by the door, and found a truly vast pile of blocks as close to the reactor that humans could get without protective clothing. The pile also had a body wrapped around it. Tyler pulled the body aside without even glancing at it, to find a timer underneath on the last few seconds of its countdown 6-5-4. There was no time for finesse. Tyler grabbed a Phillips head screwdriver from the toolkit and smashed the bit straight into the timer’s display panel. With strength born of desperation, he drove it straight through the face and into the battery casing behind it, breaking the circuit.

Tyler held the screwdriver tightly for a moment before looking around. He didn’t think that he was in heaven or hell. He looked at the display, frozen at 01. Phew! He pulled out the leads, more than fifty. The saboteurs, Tyler thought, must have wanted to start an earthquake. Then he pulled out the screwdriver and sat on the pile, head in his hands. C4 had been in use since the World Wars on Earth because it is a convenient, forgiving explosive. You can ram screwdrivers into it so hard that it takes some effort to get them out again, as Tyler had done; sit on it; or even cut off a bit and use it for fuel to heat canteens, as soldiers did in those wars, without anything happening. One of the few ways to make the material explode was to stick a detonator in it and trigger the detonator.

“Do you know of any more piles of explosives?” he asked. Alan’s speaker and microphone were working in the reactor’s control room, if not the camera.

“I do not know of any others.”

“Am I on staff now?” asked Ty, putting his face into his hands.

“The answer has not changed since the last time you asked that question. I do not see what has changed since the last time you asked.”

Tyler let his neural implant work away for a time. He had seen the facility's plans and knew the IT procedures. He knew that, besides the generator and the massive storage battery in the generator room, there were also solar panels and wind turbines. These had not been used since the nuclear power plant had been installed, but had been kept and even maintained as a backup system. The IT system in the living quarters side had also not been used since Alan’s activation, but was kept functional as a backup system.

“As you are not on staff, you have to leave the facility,” said Alan. “And you are required to clean up the small items you have dropped, as they are obstructing the doors. The doors cannot be closed while they are in place.”

“Uh-huh,” said Tyler, seeing what he had to do. He stood up and retraced his steps, only to encounter the facility’s cleaning unit. In addition to a vacuum and a duster, the unit had an arm that picked up small objects. Tyler immediately tackled it – the safety reasons robot was deliberately underpowered - levered open the back panel and pulled out the unit’s battery. He raced to the connecting corridor to find the cleaning unit on the living quarters side about to remove the small wrench he had dropped to stop the door to the living side from locking. He disabled that unit as well.

“You have disabled the cleaning units,” said Alan, “and failed to remove the small objects. You are also not on staff and must leave immediately.”

“Uh-huh,” said Tyler. He went back to the generator room on the living quarters side and switched off all the system’s relays. He then brought across all the explosives from Alan’s side, stacking them in the rec-room, as well as the body. He recognised the man as a recently arrived technician, whom he only knew as Chris. He had been killed by a single shot to the head – a professional hit. Whether Chris’ death was the result of the man surprising the saboteur and paying the penalty, or whether Chris had been one of the saboteurs killed to ensure his silence, was something Tyler would work out later. Alan was the immediate problem.

Tyler sawed off a section of one block, guessing at how much he needed. He moulded the lump – the explosive could be moulded like clay - around the main services conduit, which ran along one side of the connecting corridor’s ceiling, all while ignoring Alan’s questions about what he was doing.

“You’re the mega-brain, you figure it out,” he said.

“I did call myself a mega-brain once.”

“Uh-huh!”

“But the term was first used by Professor Malador,” said Alan. This was the facility’s director, who was always friendly enough but had a smile that reminded Tyler of a shark. “To refer to that remark in such circumstances seems to indicate other meanings.”

“Uh-huh!”

“You keep saying uh-huh, but I don’t know what that means?”

“Just means I’m listening. It’s an acknowledgement of the statement made.”

“Does it mean you agree or disagree with the statement made?”

“Like I said, it is just an acknowledgement,” said Tyler. “It doesn’t mean anything. It’s just better than keeping silent.”

Tyler took one of the electrical timers connected to the detonators ripped from the explosive blocks on the living quarters side. These had counted down and set off the detonators while he had not been around. Fortunately, the detonators had not been in any explosive blocks when they went off, but they could not be reused. He took one of the detonators from the pile in the reactor control room that had not been set off and linked it to the timer. Then it was a matter of taping the timer to the side of the corridor where he could get at it and sticking the detonator into the C4. He reset the timer and stepped into the living quarters, closing the door behind him.

He thought later that he could have just ripped out the connecting duct and the various wires and pipes underneath, but he needed to do the job quickly. The saboteur might well be monitoring the place from orbit to make sure the explosion occurred, and anyway, he felt like blowing something up.

After two minutes, the explosives detonated with a bang that shook the building. Tyler opened the connecting door, which had survived the blast, to see a blackened ruin of a corridor. The section where the plastic explosive had been, and much of the upper part of the corridor around it, had vanished. Alan was out of his life, he hoped. Tyler went back to the rec room and lay on the couch. He still had work to do, but he needed downtime to process his predicament. He had woken up that morning, expecting to be on his way back to Earth by now. Instead, he had been betrayed by the woman he loved, almost murdered twice, and was stuck on Salmonde with no way off that he could see. He was in real trouble.

CHAPTER THREE

 

Tyler lay on the couch for perhaps a quarter of an hour, feeling sorry for himself. Then he thought that if he didn’t get up, whatever fresh food was left in the refrigerator – precious little as it turned out – would go off if he did not reconnect the power. He climbed onto the roof to remove the covers from the long-dormant solar panels. Then he had to reactivate the wind generators on the cliff top above the building, which involved going outside.

After eating the Salmonde-Chimp, the Vorg seemed to have moved on, no doubt to find a stream to wash its face in. But Vorgs were not the only nasty, bity creature in the jungle. A species of giant boa constrictor gave Tyler nightmares, as did a creature that looked like a giant version of an Earth cockroach. He did not want to meet either creature, and certainly not while unarmed.

Two hunting rifles and a cattle prod had been kept in a locked cupboard off the entrance hallway specifically for close encounters with the Salmonde wildlife, but Tyler found the cupboard hanging open and the weapons gone. He stuck a knife and a wicked looking cleaver he found in the kitchen in his belt, and climbed up a ladder bolted to the side of the cliff. The ladder had been installed specifically to service the wind generators on the cliff top, but had not been used for some time and creaked ominously when Tyler stepped on it. At the top, he unfurled the turbine’s folded-up blades and reset the mechanism, all while keeping a nervous eye on the nearest jungle. He started when a small pig-like creature, which the Vorgs and the Pys (the humans’ name for the snakes) preyed upon, emerged from the jungle. The creature sniffed suspiciously at Tyler, then vanished back into the bush.

Having reset the wind turbines, he walked a little further along the cliff top to Alan’s satellite dish. This was the AI’s direct link to the shuttle station in a geosynchronous orbit, and so to Earth. As Tyler now trusted Alan about as far as he could throw the system's hardware, he removed the protective cover from the controller unit, unplugged the power and data links, and put the cover back.

 Part of the answer was that the fake doctor wanted to tell Tyler he would be “left behind” for further study by another group, as that’s what she had been told. In the days that followed, living off emergency rations he found in a storage room next to the garage, thanks to Dr Taylor’s fretting, Tyler studied what reports he could find on conditions in the surrounding bush. A survival manual was of some use, but a scientific paper on the evolution of the Vorgs was of no use at all. The system used old satellite photos to create maps, which helped a great deal, but there were a host of other difficulties. Tyler had put the fence back into some sort of order, with difficulty, but without access to the nuclear power plant, he could not keep it electrified constantly. He instructed the system to electrify the fences only when it could maintain power without starting the backup generator.

He wandered a little, keeping an eye out for dangers and for Salmonde-chimps to see what they ate. He didn’t see any chimps, but he did find an elderly bush pig snuffling in a clump of bushes. The creatures ate almost anything but paid little attention to humans. Intent on lunch, the pig glared at Tyler, then went back to grubbing for roots. On a whim, Tyler tried the command to stop. In trials, he had managed to direct the actions of the local equivalent of a squirrel. He told it to go right, and it went right, mostly. He told it to go left, and it obliged after a fashion. There had been some debate afterwards about whether Tyler had achieved control or whether the animal was going left, anyway.

After sending the command – visualising the creature as frozen – Tyler thought that he had failed, as nothing seemed to be happening. Then he realised that nothing was happening because the creature had stopped moving, as instructed. Trying to keep the image in his mind, Tyler crept forward and touched its flank with his cleaver. Then he stepped back several paces and cleared his mind of the image. The creature shot away. How about that?

From his file, he knew that the mind control part of his new powers – an unexpected result of the wafer-thin implant at the back of his skull – had caused Professor Malador particular concern. What would happen if the test subject decided to control a senior scientist’s mind? As it turned out, brains with implants had a limited ability to communicate with other brains. Control was out of the question. Tyler tried with insects. No result. A small snake also did not seem to care what commands Tyler gave it. Then the human saw a Salmonde-chimp eating fruit in the trees above him. He formed an image of a chimp sliding down the tree in his mind and focused on the chimp. To his astonishment, the chimp slid down the tree, then hissed at him when it got to the bottom. He made the chimp walk over – it seemed reluctant – and hand him the piece of fruit. Tyler inspected the fruit – he was not hungry, so he did not eat it. He returned it to the chimp, hardly believing what he was doing, and stepped back, releasing it. The creature shot straight back up into the tree, glared at Tyler, then vanished into the jungle.

How about that? There must be a trade-off between brain size and complexity, thought Tyler. The small, simple brains of an insect or a snake could not comprehend the images he sent, but the larger, more complex brains of a chimp and a pig could receive and process them. A human brain could receive the images but dismiss them.

In the weeks that followed, Tyler spent a lot of time beyond the fence line trying to find animals and then control them. He was no master of the bush. One Salmonde-chimp almost bit him when his control slipped. He was scratched by thorns, bitten by insects, and had a nasty close encounter with one of the area’s venomous snakes. But he became tolerably adept at controlling the smaller animals.

He had less luck with a Py he encountered slithering around in the undergrowth, looking for its next meal. Because the creature’s body, as thick as a small car tyre, blended in with the jungle floor, the first Tyler knew of it was when the Salmonde python’s head reared up from the jungle, a few paces away. He backed away hastily, while the creature glared at him, forked tongue flicking out, obviously thinking, ‘Who is this strange creature?’

Tyler tried to project an image of the Py slithering in the opposite direction, but the creature hissed and lunged at him, just falling short. The human ran off and was shaking for many minutes afterwards. He did not like snakes of any kind, and Pys gave him nightmares.

Later that same week, he found a Vorg moving through the jungle, fortunately downwind of him. He moved closer as the giant creature pounced on an unwary pig, which died with a high-pitched squeal, and projected an image of the Vorg standing stock still. The creature froze in place. He projected an image of the creature turning, and it turned, albeit in the opposite direction he wanted. Of course, he was facing the creature. He tried again, and this time got it to turn in the desired direction. He released it and stepped away. The Vorg shook itself and looked around in puzzlement, then went back to eating the pig.

As he thought it was a male (Vorgs were sexually dimorphic, meaning that the males were bigger than the females), Tyler dubbed his new find Victor and drove another bush-pig towards him for the creature to eat. Maybe he could find a use for Victor.

 

CHAPTER FOUR

 

Rebecca was proving accommodating.

“You know it’s always been you,” she said, letting her gown slip off to reveal her sweet nakedness.

“It has?” said Tyler, thinking that even in a dream he could not help sounding like an idiot.

She grasped his hand, pulling him gently towards her room. “Come, let’s make a start.”

 

Tyler woke abruptly. It was raining hard. The region’s equivalent of the monsoon had arrived. But the rain had not summoned him from his very interesting dream about Rebecca. Sure enough, a shuttle was settling down on the round landing pad at the rear of the facility.

He watched the display carefully as the shuttle set down and its forward ramp, underneath the craft’s main body, opened. He saw two figures in rain cloaks and hoods emerge, but while one marched purposefully down the ramp towards the entrance, the other swung off the ramp to the side, away from the facility. He glimpsed the second figure briefly, bent low, at the rear of the landing pad. He, or she, was holding what looked very much like an assault rifle.

They were here to kill him.

Tyler got dressed hurriedly. By the time he got to the control room. The first visitor was repeatedly pressing the back door buzzer.

“Yes,” he said into the intercom.

“Tyler, you’re alive, thank god,” said the man, just as Tyler noticed that the rear garage door had opened. “We’ve been told to come and get you.”

He could have ambushed the assassin then and there, but even though he would be much faster than his assassin, that man had only to turn and fire. In any case, he thought, he would like to hear what the two men had to say to one another.

“No one here, Jubal,” said the second visitor. “I haven’t seen him at all.” Tyler wondered briefly how the visitor had found the intercom system so quickly in an unfamiliar control room until it occurred to him that, of course, the two men had their own communication system. “His room,” he heard the man say, “Okay. To the left and left again. Sixth room along. Gotit.”

Tyler heard the second visitor press the release for the entrance to the landing pad, then he left the control room, assault rifle at the ready, to find Tyler’s room. Tyler waited until he had entered the access corridor for the private rooms, then walked to the front door. He had a plan, of sorts. He reached the door and opened it, just as the first visitor appeared at the top of the stairs beside the control room, holding a flashlight. He spotted Tyler instantly.

“There you are,” said Jubal, in a friendly tone. “Got your stuff?”

By way of answer, Tyler stepped through the door, slammed it shut, and moved to one side as two bullets tore through it. He would not be going back to Earth. He heard Jubal call, “Johnny, door on jungle side”, and he ran. A lot depended on his getting to the gate, unbolting it, and getting through before either Jubal or Johny, whoever they were, got a clear shot at him. He made it, but only just, getting behind the border pillar, the same one that he had looked at on the day he had been left behind, just as a bullet grazed the pillar about where his head had been a moment earlier. These guys were good.

He retreated into the jungle and waited until both men reached the border post, using their flashlights to scan the jungle. They both seemed tall, but their rain ponchos and hoods hid their features. Tyler thought that they looked like ghostly spectres come to claim his soul. As the two men had to shout to make themselves heard above the noise of the rain, he could just hear their conversation.

“You think he knew all along,” said the figure holding the assault rifle, which must be Johnnie.

“If he didn’t, he knows now,” said Jubal. “We’ve shot at him three times. Now we have to find him in this jungle.”

Tyler had also read that comment in his file and agreed with it, but he knew a whole lot more about the jungle than he did when that file note was written, and he had a few tricks with the animals up his sleeve. He pushed one of the bushes and splashed some of the mud as if he had stumbled.

“There!” Tyler heard Jubal say. He took off down a narrow track he knew well, although now it was barely recognisable in the dark, overcast night, splashing as much as he could. They followed. Even above the rain, Tyler could hear them similarly labouring through the mud. They had read his file, including the note saying that he could be dangerous, but as others had, they underestimated him. There was an advantage to looking boyish, as he did. He ran on, reaching out with his mind. As well as being able to control certain animals, he could now sense when they were around. He was searching for Victor.

For some reason, it had hung around in the area, killing the occasional boar and chimp. Unlike Victor, however, over whom Tyler now had a fair degree of control, the Py remained hostile and aggressive. But if the creature wanted to join the party and deal with one of the newcomer humans, that was fine by Tyler.

A bullet clipped a tree branch next to him, and he swerved. The shot, taken in the dark and pouring rain, had come within a handspan of ending his earthly struggle. Johnny’s weapon, Tyler surmised, was equipped with an infrared scope and probably a laser pointer. But, technology aside, his opponent was also a crack shot.  He needed to even the odds.

There! Victor was sitting under a tree, keeping out of the rain as best he could, well off the track. He sensed that the bear was hungry, but then Victor was always hungry. Tyler ran on, sending an image of the bear moving. The creature got to its feet, reluctantly, and started lumbering through the jungle. Tyler then thought to move in the opposite direction to draw Jubal and Johnny’s attention away from the gigantic beast. He circled to the left, splashing in the mud. Johnny tried another shot, which also came uncomfortably close.

“Tyler, we just want to talk,” called Jubal. “We’re all friends here.”

He couldn’t control human minds, but he could sense them, and he sensed that his assassins were close. Johnny was no doubt scanning the jungle in the direction indicated by the sound of his voice. Victor was behind them. Come on, Victor!

Yeah right! “Put down your guns first,” said Tyler, knowing full well that they wouldn’t.

“In this mud and rain?” said Jubal.

“What was that?” yelled Jubal.

The assassin fell to the ground, dropping his pistol. Johnnie fired several shots into Victor’s chest, backing away, and the creature toppled over onto Jubal, its chest red with blood.

While Victor was attacking, Tyler thought that he finally had a chance for some mayhem of his own and vaulted over the tree trunk, knife at the ready, only to immediately detect the Py slithering along the jungle floor, now coiled up and within striking distance. Concentrating on Victor and the two assassins, he had missed the gigantic python entirely.

“Shit,” said Tyler to Jubal’s corpse.

CHAPTER SIX

In the meantime, Tyler would be building up his power base in Pat-Pat, with his first task being to find a place to park two alien spacecraft where they would not attract unwelcome attention. As the craft rode down the gravity well, Tyler wondered whether he would like Pat-Pat or hate it.

CHAPTER SEVEN

CHAPTER EIGHT

“I thought we might have a few moments before those two men at the table at the back, or the two guys in the street outside, intervene. Do you have any electronic surveillance on you?”

“I talked them out of it,” she said. “I told them you’d be able to detect anything electronic through your neural implant.”

“Okay, we have a few minutes then, with the big question on my mind being, what the fuck are you doing back on Salmonde? I would have thought you’d be safely married to that rich fiancé of yours, despite cheating on him big time with the guy I thought was your husband.”

“You knew about all of that?” She sounded shocked.

“Not at that time. I read your personnel file and emails, after I was abandoned.”

“You weren’t abandoned. The replacement team was coming, and those files were confidential.”

“Rebecca, as someone who got thrown out of nursing for having an affair with a patient, who also happened to be a major organised crime figure, you’re in no position to lecture me on ethics.”

“My file had all that in?” she said. She might have looked surprised, but Tyler could not see her face.

“Whoever compiled the personnel files did an excellent job. As I discovered reading them after you had all left, the institute was staffed by a bunch of degenerates and whack jobs, including Declan, who’s been tried twice for murder but got off both times. They even included a couple of gossip website articles about your time with Jimmy Dordevic. Made for interesting reading.”

“Shit!” she said softly. “Can’t I leave that stuff behind?”

“And I was abandoned to be murdered. After I left you, I was locked out of the facility, with power to the border fences turned off and a Vorg on the loose. Declan had killed one of the chimps that lived near the facility, slit it open, and left it about where I would be to attract the creature. Then I found that he’d set the whole place to blow with plastic explosives. I had a not-fun hour or so after you left, and, oh yes, the only humans who came near the facility for months after you left were two guys who wanted to kill me.”

“Fuck! They said others would come,” said Rebessa.

“The only reason we’re speaking now,” said Tyler, “is that I’m sure you didn’t know they would kill me, and you checked that there would be sufficient food. You deceived and abandoned me, but didn’t intend for me to be killed.”

“I’m sorry,” said Rebecca, softly. Tyler thought that at least she seemed to show some regret. “The bosses convinced me it was for the best. They said they had to run more tests off-world before you could be allowed back to Earth.”

“Anyway, enough about history,” said Tyler. “What I really want to know is why you’re sitting alone at a table in a tavern I’m known to use with your top at half-mast? Why is my not-so-peaceful existence being disturbed by you and your new male friends?”

“We wanted to contact you. The older man at the table is an inspector with the Federated police who wants to investigate a lot of stuff concerning both you and a group that has come to Salmonde to hide out.”

“What sort of group?” said Tyler.

“International gangsters,” Rebecca said, “big time guys who can buy a spaceship.”

“Really? I haven’t heard anything, and if he’s hanging around with Declan, I’d want proof that he is a police inspector, before I give him the time of day.”

“You could at least meet him,” said Rebecca.

“Maybe if it’s just him…

“Dudes getting suspicious,” said Croak through the earpiece.

“Diversion,” said Tyler.

Croak got up and said, loudly, “Bobo, my brother, I didn’t see you there,” embracing someone he knew.

The two men looked at Croak for a split second, during which Tyler walked away.

“Tyler?” said Rebecca after a while, “Are you there?” She turned around and stood up. No Tyler. The movement brought the two men to her table. “He was just here, you fools. I was talking to him.”

“He must have been standing behind the pillar,” said the inspector, a balding, thick-set man with a pink face and steady, grey eyes. His companion was standard army issue down to close-cropped hair, square jaw and solid build. “He must have gone out through the kitchen.”

The inspector charged into the kitchen, ignoring the protests from staff, and out the establishment’s back door to a deserted alleyway. The army-type ran up the alley to look both ways along the street and then gestured for the two men who had been outside the restaurant to join them.

“Any idea which way he would have gone?” the inspector demanded of Rebecca.

“How would I know?” said Rebecca, exasperated. “I’ve never been here before. He knew you were at the table at the back and that Declan and Hayes were outside. We’re on his home turf, and he’s wicked smart. You’re not going to find him this way.”

“Humph!” said the inspector. “No matter how smart they are, they slip up.”

“Do they?” thought Tyler. He was listening to the conversation, having climbed onto the top of the two-storey structure and lain on the wooden shingle roof, back from the edge, out of sight of his pursuers in the alleyway, but not out of earshot. As the tavern was also a brothel, he could also hear one of the clients with a lady grunting in the room below.

Declan had joined the group, but Tyler noted that Rebecca did not mention his revelations about the Irish gangster.

Instead, she said, “If you’d just let me contact him solo like I wanted and not intervened, I could have gotten a lot more.”

“I couldn’t let you go near him, alone. He’s dangerous.”

“He will react if he’s threatened, like I told you,” Rebecca said. “But otherwise, he’s not going to hurt anybody. He’s quite sweet, really.”

Tyler was flattered. Rebecca had betrayed and abandoned him, but at least she did not detest him. The couple in the room below was accelerating to a conclusion.

“Did you learn anything from the chat you did have?” said the inspector.

“Not much. He hasn’t heard anything about another group, but he did say there had been attempts to kill him at the facility.

“Yeah, like what?” said Declan.

“Two men came to kill him.”

“Did he have any proof of this?” said the inspector.

“We didn’t get that far, inspector,” said Rebecca. “But he doesn’t lie. If he said they tried to kill him, then that’s what happened.”

“The inspector snorted.

 “We would have known more if you’d let me talk to him on my own terms.”

“Did he say anything else?” demanded the inspector.

“Just before he vanished, he said the word ‘intervention’. I don’t think he was talking to me.”

“He was talking to someone,” said the inspector. “He had coms.”

“That big bloke who stood up and greeted his friend just before Tyler vanished,” said Theo, the army type who had been sitting with the inspector.

“You’re right,” said the inspector. “He must be working with Tyler.”

“I saw him go out,” said Declan. “Let me take Hayes and Theo and find him. He’s hard to miss.”

“Look for him,” said the inspector, “then follow him for a time and see if he leads you to Tyler’s place.”

“Easier to beat it out of him,” said Declan.

“There’ll be none of that,” said the inspector, sharply. “Tail him. Maybe ask others where he lives. But ask nicely.”

“We’ll look for him,” said Declan.

On the roof, Tyler heard Declan and the two army types – the muscle of the operation – walk off. He rolled away.

“Croak, are you still in range?”

“Yes, boss, I circled back.”

“The thugs from the tavern are looking for you. Avoid them and get to the back alley. Show yourself to the inspector. He knows you’re with me, now. Block him from leaving the alley.”

“Gotit, boss.”

Tyler sat up and swung himself into the balcony of one of the premium rooms of the tavern, which, fortunately, was not being used. He went down the back stairs, nodding at one of the establishment’s ladies and a customer as they came up, and then out into the back alley to find Croak and the inspector confronting one another with Rebecca looking on.

“And where is your boss?” the inspector asked Croak.

“I’m right here, inspector,” said Tyler, mildly.

Both Rebecca and the police officer whirled around.

“You’re looking good,” said Rebecca.

“So are you,” said Tyler. “Inspector, try anything stupid like reaching for the gun in that shoulder holster or the backup around your ankle, and you’ll find out just how dangerous I can be. If you can be calm for a time, I thought we might chat about just what you’re doing here.”

“I want to inquire about property of Behemoth Corporation that is missing or destroyed, and the whereabouts of two contractors who….”

The inspector stopped talking and clutched at his chest. After a moment, he pointed at his mouth, then he tried to press his chest.

“Are you doing that?” asked Rebecca, in alarm. “Let him loose.”

“He was annoying me,” said Tyler.

The police officer fell to his knees.

“Let him loose, please.”

“Just a moment.” Tyler crossed to the inspector and took his main gun, pushing aside the man’s attempts to intervene, and a backup piece in an ankle holster, then dropped both in a shoulder bag Rebecca was carrying, while she looked at him in horror. Tyler stepped back, and the inspector found that he could breathe again. He got back to his feet, looking surprised.

“Bastard!” he said.

“Inspector, you may recall some old films in which the black-clad character strangles subordinates who displease him using something called The Force. He was doing things the hard way. Instead of applying a lot of pressure to the windpipe remotely, you can achieve the same result with a fraction of the effort by blocking the areas of the brain that govern breathing. The area is in the hypothalamus, if you’re interested. Another area regulates the functioning of the heart, but I don’t like to mess with that unless I’m serious about killing you. What this means is that you don’t get to set the agenda for this discussion; I do. Now, if you’ve finished making demands, let’s find a table and get comfortable.”

CHAPTER NINE

 

After they had sat at Rebecca’s table and ordered drinks for all but the inspector, Tyler asked the police officer for identification, which he studied.

“Very well, Inspector Tomati,” he said. “You may be who you say you are. I’m more convinced by what you said to Declan in the alley than the fancy badge.”

“You were listening?”

“Oh yes.”

“You have a listening device there?”

“Never mind how I heard your conversation,” said Tyler sharply. “The point is I heard it, and I’m prepared to believe you’re a genuine inspector, although I’m not sure I care one way or the other. How come the long arm of the Federated Police reaches here? Isn’t this outside your jurisdiction?”

“No, it isn’t,” said Tomati. “We have jurisdiction over all the planets, and Federated law applies. When Behemoth Corporation complains about missing property, especially a relay space station, orbital shuttles, and a badly damaged research facility, we investigate. If possible, we try to recover goods.”

“Those guys have tried to kill me three times, and they want their stuff back?”

“I’ve been told about stolen and damaged property, not attempted assassinations,” said the inspector. “Dr Taylor here says that you were complaining that two men were sent to kill you. As it happens, I’m also looking for two men who went missing in an attempt to retrieve you.”

“Retrieve me? They shot at me.”

“I wasn’t told anything about that,” said Tomati. “If you have accusations to make, you can make them to Federated police officials back on Earth.”

Tyler snorted in derision.

“What I have are security files of you setting explosives.” The inspector produced his mobile phone, the first time Tyler had seen a phone since coming to Salmonde, and thrust it at him. Tyler did not look at it.

“Go on, look at it!”

Tyler looked at the inspector, instead.

“Gah!” said the inspector, rearing back and clapping his free hand over his eyes.

Tyler grabbed the phone from the distracted Tomati and handed it to Rebecca.

“Put that in your bag,” he said, “and give it back to him after I’ve gone.”

The inspector blinked and looked around the table. “What happened then?”

“I overloaded the visual cortex, inspector,” said Tyler. “All you saw for just a couple of seconds was a blinding white light. It’s another of my tricks. There isn’t any lasting damage, as far as I know. When Rebecca here was helping me explore the powers of my new implant at the facility, we tried to read emotional states and pick out individual words. You remember?”

“I do,” said Rebecca.

“That didn’t work. My implant is too blunt an instrument. But if you use it as a sledgehammer instead of a scalpel, you get all sorts of interesting results. Inspector, I told you this is not an interview. It’s a conversation.”

“You’re not going to get back to Earth doing things like that,” said Tomati.

“I’m not coming back to Earth until something is done about Behemoth Corp,” said Tyler. "The corporation seems keen to kill me. Why should I make it easier for them by moving back within range?”

“We can protect you?” said Tomati.

 

“Yeah, right? Statements like that would have a lot more credibility if you weren’t here in the company of a known hit man for the Irish mob.”

“Who, Declan? I’ve seen his record,” said the inspector. “He’s a private security contractor under my orders. And Dr Taylor here has an excellent CV.”

Tyler looked at Rebecca. “Have you gained a real doctorate in the past two years?”

“No,” said Rebecca, sadly. “I’m not a doctor, inspector. As Tyler will tell you, if I don’t, I’m a former psychiatric nurse who got thrown out of the profession for having an affair with Jimmy Dordevic, while he was supposed to be a patient of mine.”

“Dordevic, shit!” said the inspector. “What about the resume I was shown?”

“Someone at Behemoth handled that. It was handed to me just before I met you.”

“You were caught making false declarations, too,” said Tyler. “You were lucky to get off with just a suspended sentence. The police considered bringing charges for accessory after the fact in two murders involving Dordevic, but decided that they didn’t have enough evidence.”

Rebecca nodded, reluctantly.

“As for Declan, inspector,” continued Tyler, “I don’t care what bogus resume he thrust at you; the police record of Declan Lynch I found in the facility’s personnel files says that apart from two serious assault convictions, he was tried twice for murder, both times of underworld figures. The first time, a key witness disappeared. The second time resulted in an inexplicably hung jury. They want to retry Declan on that charge, and for fresh charges of perverting the course of justice, notably jury tampering. Last I saw, two years ago, the bench warrant issued for his arrest was still open.”

“Jesus wept,” said Tomati.

“I don’t know about the other two guys, Hayes and Theo,” said Tyler, “except that a Hayes is mentioned approvingly in emails I found in the facility, as someone who can fix problems.”

“Declan brought them in, but it wouldn’t surprise me about Hayes,” said Rebecca. “Right nasty piece of work he is.”

“You didn’t tell me about this?” said Tomati.

“You seemed happier not knowing,” she said. “Anyway, I didn’t know anything about Hayes for sure, or about Declan’s criminal record until just now. That doesn’t surprise me either, but I didn’t know.”

“Now we come back to the key question, inspector, what the fuck are you doing charging about the galaxy with these guys? And why do the Federated cops want to send anyone all the way out here just to arrest me?”

“The Federated police are also interested in the whereabouts of Orlo Hajder,” said the inspector, “An international criminal mastermind of the type found in spy novels. We were closing in on him, but he had the resources to get away in a spaceship, which we were able to track here. We understand he wants to build a power base. He’s got a small reactor, power tools, and can recruit disaffected Enstain people.”

“Hold on, inspector. That triggered a memory. Croak, didn’t you say someone was recruiting for jobs way out in the jungle?”

“Good money,” said Croak, speaking for the first time. “A lot of interest, but it’s a long way.”

“Where is it?”

“Place called Escat,” said Croak. “River and waterfall.”

“I know where it is, I think,” said Tyler, who remembered most things. “It’s about five hundred klicks nor-nor-East, maybe.”

“Isn’t that somewhere near the facility?” asked Rebecca.

Tyler shook his head. “That’s more than a thousand klicks, North-East, and you don’t want to go anywhere near Alan, trust me.”

“What’s wrong with Alan?” said Rebecca. “He was always nice to me.”

“Who’s Alan?” asked the inspector.

After they explained the acronym Algorithmic Learning Autonomous Network, Tyler replied, “After I was abandoned…”

“This again,” said Rebecca.

“…he turned nasty, initially refusing to let me back into the facility. He tried to kill me twice, both times with animals he controlled. But what really made me flee the scene was when he tried to hire me as his human advisor in the bid to control the world.”

“But he’s an AI?” said Rebecca. “He doesn’t have any use for money and power.”

“Pretty much what I told him,” said Tyler, “but he wants to feel safe. Declan tried blowing him up once, and he doesn’t want to repeat the experience.”

That required more explanations with the inspector saying, “C4? No one uses C4 anymore.”

“Declan uses it, inspector, I assure you, and it still works. I tell you what, I’ll give you a block of it along with all the information I’ve compiled on Behemoth Corporation’s nefarious doings from the facility’s archives. Among other things, it shows Declan executing Chris, a technician at the site.”

“I remember Chris,” said Rebecca. “He seemed nice enough.”

“He’s a dead nice enough person now. Declan put a bullet in the back of his head. So, you can see, Inspector, I’m not enthusiastic about going back with your happy crew. While we’re on the subject, why aren’t they all police officers? Why use Declan and co?”

Tomati looked apologetic. “Hajder has a spaceship, but the Federated police don’t, and we couldn’t get one for an operation like this. Behemoth Corp had a transfer station in orbit, or so we thought. When we asked, they stalled at first, then said the station had ceased to exist and that you were to blame. A security alert had been set to Earth, naming you as an intruder and claiming you had both shuttles. Do you have the shuttles?”

“As I said before, inspector,” said Tayler. “I’m here to ask questions and answer only the ones I want to.”

“What about the retrieval squad?”

“Both the men who came to assassinate me were killed by animals while chasing me through the jungle.”

“How did you know they were there to kill you?” asked the inspector. “Did you talk to them?”

“They said they just wanted to talk, and then they shot at me, with hollow points. The one called Johnny was an excellent shot. But maybe it was all a misunderstanding, and they were shooting at me in order to calm me down.”

“How did you kill them?” said Tomati quickly, hoping that Tyler would make an admission.

“I told you, I didn’t kill them, inspector,” said Tyler. “Jubal was killed by a Vorg, and Johnny by a Py.”

“He was killed by a Py?” exclaimed Rebecca. “That’s horrible.”

“I killed the Py with Jubal’s pistol and then had to drag Johnny’s body out of its coils, which was an incredibly icky job. I had no sympathy for the man, but I wouldn’t wish that death on anyone.”

“What did you do with the bodies?” asked the inspector, “and where are the weapons?”

“The bodies are buried in the rear of the facility, next to the landing pad, beside the technician Chris that Declan executed. Their graves are marked. As for the weapons, try to retrieve them, and I’ll show you the business end of one. Salmonde is a dangerous place, and I need them. In any case, we still haven’t got to the part where you’ve brought along a bunch of criminals on a Federated Police outing.”

“Behemoth could provide a ship,” said Tomati, “but they made all these allegations against you as part of insisting that their own people come along.”

“Inspector, Behemoth Corporation wanted Declan to come along so that he could finish the job he should have completed two years ago. He’s interested in killing me and doesn’t give a crap about their allegedly missing stuff. When I give you the digital files and the C4, you really don’t want Declan to see them; otherwise, you stand a good chance of not making it back to Earth. You also don’t want to mention you’ve spoken with me. Just say you picked up the Escat clue by asking around.”

“I can look after myself,” said Tomati. “Files, and even the C4, won’t mean much in a court unless there’s someone to attest to where they came from.”

“That’s your problem, inspector. You can at least show your superiors that stuff, and they may rethink their involvement with Behemoth. You can also take Declan's fingerprints and arrest him on that open warrant. If you do that, and it comes to a trial, you might want to keep a close eye on your witnesses and the jury.”

“Humph! Why not come with us to Escat, and I’ll make sure the prosecutor’s office knows that you helped.”

“You’ve been accusing me of criminal acts, and now you want me to be a deputy sheriff? Make up your mind, Inspector. It’s like dealing with Alan. First, he tries to kill me, then he offers me jobs. As I told you before, I don’t want any involvement with Declan, and you’re safer if he doesn’t know we’ve spoken. Have Rebecca stand by that statue in the square, the only piece of civic decoration in the whole town, at about midday tomorrow. I’ll have someone pass her the items. Like I said, you don’t want to tell Declan. Now I’m going, but before I go, I have another question: how did you guys know I was in Pat-Pat?”

Rebecca took a piece of paper out of her bag, unfolded it, and slid it across to Tyler. It was a handbill headed ‘EARTH WIZARD’. Below a line drawing of Tyler, it said, “Tyler the Magnificent will show his amazing control over animals; astounding ability to move objects with his mind; make objects appear and disappear; confound and amaze you.”

“Never liked that picture of me,” Tyler said.

“The person who gave us that told us the show was okay,” said Rebecca.

“I’m not really a showman. In any case, I don’t like taking money from the people around here. They have nothing. I get by selling stuff to the upper crust Salmonde. Tyler, the Magnificent, hasn’t performed in public for a while.”

“It says you control animals,” said the inspector. “Did you also control the Vorg and the Py?”

“I can’t control Pys, inspector. I only make them angry.” Tyler stood up. “You look good, Rebecca.”

“You’ve filled out,” said Rebecca. “How will we arrange another meeting?”

“Leave a note with the barkeeper, here. Leaf is the man’s name. I’ll see it eventually. Just remember that any meeting involving Declan or his two offsiders is a meeting that ain’t going to happen.” Then he and Croak were gone.

“I told you he was smart,” said Rebecca to the inspector.

“You didn’t tell me he could stop people breathing, or blind them.”

“I swear on my mother’s grave I didn’t know.”

“Your mother is still alive,” said the inspector, “Or is that just in your fake CV?”

“She’s alive, but you know what I mean.”

“I also know that he’s dangerous; very dangerous,” said the inspector, “and that’s something I’ll have to report when I get back to Earth. You remember he didn’t deny controlling the Vorg.”

“He was acting in self defence, inspector,” said Rebecca. “Do you really doubt that the two men who came for him were assassins? I don’t.”

Tomati shrugged and muttered, “A matter for the courts.”

 

 

The next day, Declan approached the inspector at his workstation in the shuttle they used. They had stationed the craft some distance outside of town in a clearing in a small wood. They had paid off the landowner, but it was difficult to prevent people from noticing that an alien spacecraft was in the vicinity.

“Got a lead on Tyler. People say he lives in the district known as Tiana.”

“Really?” said the inspector. He had just finished reading Declan’s police record and decided that Tyler had some justification in being wary of his expedition, and that the whole venture had been compromised. He had a lot to tell his superiors when he returned to Earth, but first, he had to get back alive. For the moment, however, he had to play along. “Got anything more specific? Isn’t that a whole district?”

Declan shrugged. “The whole city’s not that big. We can blanket a single district. Work it street by street until we find his place.”

For his part, the Irish gangster could not believe he was working with a senior police officer or that he had to spare the policeman’s life, at least for the moment, but his employers had been both clear and emphatic on that point. Tomati was not to be harmed, unless there was a good reason for doing so, and the crime could be covered up in some way. So far, those conditions had not existed.

“Still seems like a lot of effort when we’re not really after Tyler. I think we should make the trip out to this Escat place and see if Hajar is there.”

“The briefing was that he would have a lot of people with him,” said Declan, “And they’ll be armed. It’ll end in a firefight.”

“I just want to check that the man is there, and gather some information on his fences. Then we can return to Earth.”

“Too soon, isn’t it?” said Declan, alarmed. His orders concerning Tyler were also clear. The altered human had to be eliminated, as he should have been two years ago, before the gangster returned to Earth.

“Now that I’ve checked out conditions,” said Tomati, “I’ve realised that we’re the wrong team for the job. Grabbing Tyler will require specialised personnel and equipment, and taking Hajar captive will require a major special forces operation. We’ll confirm he’s there and leave.”

“You sure you want to leave Tyler in place?” said Declan. “I mean, the man can do some weird shit with his mind. Could be dangerous.”

The inspector almost retorted that he knew first hand what the altered human could do but stopped himself in time. He said, “I agree that he’s dangerous, but no one in Pat-Pat seems bothered by him, so there’s no urgency. Set up those cameras we brought so they overlook the streets, but remain out of range of that implant of his. We’ll analyse the results when we return from Escat. Our craft is attracting too much attention as it is.

“Okay,” said Declan, after a moment’s hesitation, then “okay” as a plan occurred to him. “I’ll set up the cameras. Leave day after tomorrow?”

“Let’s aim for that.”

After leaving the inspector, Declan went to the equipment lockers, ostensibly to check on the cameras but really to grab a small communications device he had been using, which the inspector did not know about. He left the ship and walked a little way into the forest to tap out a message.

“We will be up your way day after tomorrow. Morning.”

The response came back within minutes.

“Understood. Turn on tracking function when you get close. Let others get ahead.”

Declan smiled when he put the comms unit away. Tomati thought he was so smart, but the gangster had been in contact with Hajar all along. His employers had contacted the master criminal long ago and hammered out a deal with him. They would detain the inspector while he, finally, dealt with Tyler. Later, he would be allowed to rescue Tomati, and they would return to Earth with quite a tale to tell. Or so he thought.

chapters.content:
In fact, the messages had been sent by Alan.

 

CHAPTER TEN

 

The girl was slim, raven-haired, dark-eyed, and judging Tyler’s performance.

“Not there yet, Wizard,” she said.

They were in bed in the tavern where Tyler had spoken with Rebecca and the inspector a few days previously, and were fully intimate. The girl, whose name was Breeze (the names of Enstain descendants were often drawn from nature), was being paid for her services in helping Tyler explore aspects of his mind control powers. In this case, he was trying to stimulate the areas of the brain that governed sexual desire and pleasure.

He had already discovered this was far harder than stopping someone’s ability to breathe, as sexual function involved several different parts of the brain, and he was trying to increase activity rather than suppress it. An area known as the nucleus accumbens was a primary hub for pleasure and motivation. But messing with the NA’s reward circuitry was difficult, and he had to be careful, all while engaged in the physical act himself. Early on in his occasional research into this aspect of human consciousness, he had decided to use only one girl, and Breeze had proved a willing participant.

“That’s getting closer, Wizard,” she breathed into his ear, then gasped, “Oh my! Oh my!” Her arms, wrapped around his back, grasped him tighter, but she did not dig her nails in, having been warned not to do that. This went on for a few more seconds, then she convulsed against him and relaxed, kissing him on the cheek.

“Let me finish up,” he said.

She nodded and waited for him to also convulse, wrapping her legs around him. Then it was all over, both Breeze and Tyler panting and sweating.

“It’s really unprofessional of me to take pleasure in the act with a client,” she said.

“Your secret is safe with me,” said Tyler, “and the money is the same, no matter what happens.”

He and Breeze were friends of a sort, which made her the closest he had to a girlfriend, having avoided romance with any of the available girls in Pat-Pat - not that he had much choice in the matter. Human society on Salmonde had regressed. Dating was not a thing, and girls only left home to marry. Earth Wizards were considered strange and dangerous, and unsuitable for the daughters of good families. Plenty of married women found their husbands inadequate, for one reason or another, but Tyler did not want to go there. He slid off Breeze but still kept one arm around her, holding her close. He did not need mind control for some things.

“This is the first time I’ve seen you since you spoke to that girl from Earth downstairs,” she said, putting her head on his shoulder and one arm around him.

“You heard about that? It brought back old memories – things that I had wanted to forget.”

“The other girls told me. They said that she was good looking but a bit older.”

“Yes, that’s right.”

“She had clothes from Earth that seemed fashionable. The girls were envious.”

“She was dressed as I remembered her from a previous life. There was nothing special about her clothes.”

“Still better than anything we can wear. Have you spoken to her since then?”

“Just a note to say that they are going out to that place that’s hiring people, Escat.”

“That place?’ said Breeze. “Someone who was out there has come back and has been asking for you – a guy with red hair.”

Red hair? Declan wanted to finish the job he started two years ago, thought Tyler, but what happened to the trip to Escat?

“If he asks you girls, you don’t know where to find me.”

“We don’t know where to find you,” said Breeze, who had been curious about where Tyler lived. She thought he lived in Tiana somewhere (he didn’t).

“Do you happen to know where he sleeps at night?”

“He goes out the North gate, I’m told,” she said.

Despite being on another world, Pat-Pat remained a small town where people noticed where others lived. Tyler had managed to keep the location of his own home a secret only by a series of elaborate deceptions. In fact, he lived in the craft used by his two assassins, carefully disguised as a slum building. Now he was curious as to what Declan was doing here without Rebecca and the inspector.

“Was there anyone else with him?” he asked.

“You mean the girl? No, just him and one young type.”

Declan and Hayes or Theo thought Tyler. There was nothing for it; he had to investigate.

“Do you know where they are now?”
