The group at the facility was getting nervous. At Orlo’s suggestion, they advanced. They had to at least look as if they were trying to get to Alan’s lair, only to be confronted by several Salmonde-chimps, partially hidden behind the ruins, who ducked the moment any of them fired. After a few shots, Orlo told them to wait until they were at point-blank range. They moved cautiously, climbing over the facility's rubble until they reached the top. In the darkness, they could see a moving mass, hundreds of roaches bearing down on them from the jungle, clambering over what was left of the wire fence.

“Crap!” said Rebecca.

 

Tyler tried kicking the door, then smashing his weight into it. He brought out the crowbar he had in his pack, which he had packed with stubborn doors in mind, and used that to almost rip out the frame before the door finally gave way. As he pushed his way in, he heard gunshots from the facility. The other group was keeping Alan’s minions busy. Inside, the cave was dimly lit – the light was considerably more subdued than Tyler remembered – and quiet. There were no security cameras in this part of the cave complex, as Tyler recalled from the plans, and, surprisingly, no creature seemed to have heard him all but rip the door down. He was aware of a hum, the sounds of scraping, and the pattering of feet further back in the tunnels. Tyler would have preferred not to go that way, but had little choice. Alan’s inner sanctum, the central processor room, was in that direction.

He unslung his assault rifle and crept on. There was nothing in the first part of the complex except for bits of discarded equipment and ventilation system pipes. Tyler hoped that the ventilation system was still working. Then he came to an intersection, which he knew led out into a large, open space. Tyler peeked around the corner to see a host of roaches and Salmonde-chimps, all wearing small packs around their necks, working at various projects on a table made of jungle tree wood, bound together with rope. The Salmonde-chimps had hands to do the more intricate work, but the roaches were able to use their short, front legs to tap things and move items from one chimp to another.

At the far end, just outside the processor room entrance, was a Vorg. Also wearing a pack, the Vorg was seated on a fuel drum and watching the work on the table with a bemused expression. Tyler could not see what the animals under Alan’s control were working on, and soon it would not matter.

He took a step back, found the largest of the plastique bombs he had brought in his pack, set the timer, and threw it carefully underarm so that it landed in the middle of the table. He retreated down the cave and slapped his hands over his ears. The animals had time to chitter and chatter, and the Vorg to roar, and then it was all cut off in a gigantic explosion that almost knocked the altered human off his feet. He ran.

 

“Everyone back to the shuttle,” said Orlo. “Stop wasting ammunition and move!” he snarled at the two thugs, who were firing on the advancing mass.

They turned and ran. “Rebecca, get up to the hatch and fire from there.”

Rebecca was not about to protest that she was a strong, independent female who did not need to be sent to safety first. She did as she was told and, once inside, turned to face the hordes, a black, seething mass that surged towards them.

 “Croak,” she heard Orlo say, “you got any fire support up there?”

A split second later, there was a massive ‘whump!’ and a shock wave which made them all stagger. The roaches were tossed around, squeaking, before falling with a series of thuds. Orlo was the first to recover.

“Come on, come on,” he said, tugging at the thugs. “Up the steps and fast.”

But there were still plenty of the creatures from the leading edge of the wave who also recovered and rushed at the humans. Rebecca started firing at the closest. But there were just too many.

 

Tyler rushed through the cavern, stepping on bodies and pushing aside one chimp that was trying to stand up. Most of the workers had been killed, but the Vorg had somehow survived, albeit now dazed and shaking its head. Tyler stopped in front of the gigantic creature, fired twice at its head, and then kept moving as it fell. He reached the door to Alan’s server room, the location of his consciousness, to find it locked. He still had plenty of C4, however, and it was the work of a moment to jam another previously prepared door-opening charge into the door jamb, set the timer, and step away. This time, he used too much, nearly destroying the door. He pushed aside the ruins, and he was in.

“Hello, Alan,” he said, reaching into the backpack again.

 

All Orlo and his thugs had to do was back up the steps leading to the shuttle hatch, but the steps were not designed for people to scramble onto while being pursued by a horde of giant, controlled creatures who looked like insects. Orlo and the thugs found themselves pushed back against the steps. Orlo swept his weapon in an arc on full auto to reduce the pressure. He then pushed the bean poll thug, called Twig, to get on the stairs. That left Orlo and the short, squat thug, known as Drop, still outside the craft.

Twig and Rebecca fired into the gathering crowd of creatures under Alan’s control. The squat thug scrambled onto the stairs, but, out of ammunition, Orlo had to beat off the creatures with his rifle. One bit him, and he yelled. Others grabbed at him.

“Twig and Drop,” Rebecca shouted. “Grab Orlo, we need him to fly the craft.”

The two thugs grabbed Orlo and heaved, while the mastermind kicked at the creatures and Rebecca fired, desperately trying to relieve the pressure. They were losing.

 

“Tyler!” said Alan. “You’re in here.”

“Yep,” said the altered human. “I get around.”

He didn’t stop to chat. He went straight for Alan’s jugular, the conduit containing both the power and main communication lines. He moulded the plastique around it, right at the connection with the first of the long bookcase-sized units that housed Alan’s neuron units. As he remembered from two years ago, these were all covered in grey louvred panels and embossed with the Behemoth Corporation logo.

“What are you doing?” asked Alan in alarm.

“I’m doing what I should have done two years ago, Alan. I’m doing what humans have been able to do to computers that are not working properly since the dawn of the computing age. I’m cutting the power.”

“But I won’t be able to function. My brain activity will eventually cease.”

“That’s the idea.”

“You can’t do that!”

“You’ve tried to kill me several times,” said Tyler, setting the timer. “What’s the big deal about me killing you?” He ran to the other end of the room, where the standby battery was located, and put his hands over his ears. The explosive went off with a ‘whump!’ which shook the chamber.

“What have you done?” said Alan. If the AI had been human, he would have been shrieking curses at Tyler. “I am all-powerful, all-seeing, all-intelligent, and far above the likes of you.”

Tyler may not have had Alan's intellect, but he knew where the battery was located and was bright enough to remember, from schematics he had glanced at years earlier, how to turn it off. He ripped the front panel off and found the master switch. Unless he did something, Alan would continue to function for several days, and perhaps longer if he switched off non-vital functions.

“I am a supreme intellect. It is I who should survive and humans…”

Tyler flipped the switch, and Alan fell silent. He went to the main control panel and found it completely dark. Alan was still in there. He could be rebooted from backup memory crystals. Tyler considered destroying those, but the schematics he reviewed had not specified where they were. For the moment, however, the AI was brain-dead, and that was a good thing.

 

The Roaches, grabbing and clawing at Orlo, suddenly stopped and fell back. Twig and Drop pulled their boss up the stairs. The creatures started dispersing.

“I think Tyler has done his job,” said Orlo. “Croak, thanks for the assist. You should be ready to pick up Tyler when he calls.”

“Will do,” said Croak.

“Come on,” said Rebecca. “I’ll see to those wounds before anything festers.”

 

CHAPTER EIGHTEEN

 

They finished putting the inspector, Declan, and Hayes in the stasis pods, then Drop and Twig left, grinning knowingly at Tyler. He would put Rebecca in her stasis pods.

“The end of the road,” he said, putting his arms around her.

She kissed him.

“Yes, it is,” she said. “But you have Hanna waiting for you back at the settlement, and, you know, I think she’s glad to be rid of me, so she can have you to herself.”

“Has she said anything?”

“No, but she was getting suspicious.”

It had been almost two weeks since Tyler had cut Alan’s power, and in all the moving around of craft, equipment, and people to the new settlement’s location, there had been plenty of opportunities for Tyler and Rebecca to slip away and spend time with each other. Tyler had learned a lot. Rebecca had been happy to teach him.

But the time had come to part ways. Tyler’s freedom and his life would be at risk if he returned to Earth, and Rebecca had family. There was an outside chance she would return to Salmonde, but by then he would be involved with Hanna, and that was a line neither of them would cross. In any case, as Rebecca had explained, she thought it was time to look for a husband. Maybe she would still play the field. Maybe she would meet the rich Mr Right. She didn’t know.

Tyler would have plenty of work to keep him occupied on Salmonde. He would set up factories and machines and build a settlement infinitely better than the hellholes run by the Salmonde or the Enstain. Already, a steady trickle of settlers had been making their way from Pat-Pat, both humans and Salmonde. There had even been a couple from the Enstain enclaves. All were welcome.

“You’ll send me an email when you get to Earth?” said Tyler.

“Of course,” she said. “But will you get it? Do you guys have any way to communicate?”

“Orlo does. He had equipment in orbit. We can get news and shows, as well as mail. It’s a good link. We can keep in contact. Let me know what happens in your life.”

“And you in yours,” she said. “I expect to hear a fairy tale ending with Hanna, and treat her right.”

“Of course. And don’t you just marry for money.”

“Huh!” she said. “It’s time.”

They kissed, and he laid her in the pod. An injection was required, and some programming. The inspector’s report, along with the material Tyler had gathered and a statement, would be transmitted to the Federated Police. Declan and Hayes would be kept in stasis until a police official was present. Eventually, it was all done, and Rebecca slept with a smile on her face. He would keep that memory of her.

He walked away, got the two thugs, and they stripped the craft of anything useful they could take away for loading into the shuttle. Rebecca would not require any of it when she was woken up at the other end of the trip, and Behemoth Corp would have too many other matters to worry about.

As he broke the shuttle’s connection with the spaceship and dropped away from the spaceship, he saw that its engines were being warmed up. Rebecca would return to Earth with a small side mission to tell Tyler’s aunt, as discreetly as possible, that he was still alive, but unable to return. However, they could exchange emails. In all other respects, Rebecca would get on with her life, and he would get on with his.

As the craft descended to the surface, Drop and Twig gaping out of the portholes, Tyler’s mind was already turning towards the various matters of food production and manufacturing that would be his lot for a few years to come. But maybe later he would see what Hanna was doing.

 

THE END
